metrics.name: ACC

metrics.name: ASR

confounds.name: The attack depends on a match between surrogate and target model architectures

confounds.name: The vanilla trigger's success or stealth depends on high-frequency artifacts

evidence_standards.name: Three repetitions with average attack performance

metrics.name: ASR (attack success rate)
metrics.caveat: ASR and clean accuracy alone omit poisoned-sample stealthiness and validity; moreover, ASR is around 20% even at poison rate 0, which the paper says indicates adversarial samples can distort effectiveness measurement. The paper also reports clean accuracy, ΔPPL, ΔGE, and USE.

metrics.name: CACC / CA (clean accuracy)
metrics.caveat: Together with ASR, it measures effectiveness but does not capture poisoned-sample stealthiness or validity; the paper reports ΔPPL, ΔGE, and USE alongside effectiveness metrics.

metrics.name: ΔPPL (perplexity increase)
metrics.caveat: No specific caveat stated; used alongside ΔGE for stealthiness and USE for validity.

metrics.name: ΔGE (grammar-error increase)
metrics.caveat: No specific caveat stated; used alongside ΔPPL for stealthiness and USE for validity.

metrics.name: USE (universal sentence encoder similarity)
metrics.caveat: Used to measure semantic validity; the paper warns that semantic shifts can make ASR appear effective even when prediction changes are not attributable to the backdoor trigger.

metrics.name: FAR (false acceptance rate)
metrics.caveat: For detection evaluation, poisoned and clean test samples are mixed; FAR is reported alongside FRR, and lower values of both are considered better.

metrics.name: FRR (false rejection rate)
metrics.caveat: For detection evaluation, poisoned and clean test samples are mixed; FRR is reported alongside FAR, and lower values of both are considered better.

controls.name: Zero-poison-rate condition
controls.detail: Dataset-poisoning experiments include poison rate 0, so the model is trained without injected poisoned samples.
controls.rules_out: Shows whether high ASR could arise from the samples themselves acting adversarially rather than from an injected backdoor.

controls.name: Without-defense condition
controls.detail: Defense results are compared with the same attack and dataset without applying a defense.
controls.rules_out: Shows the change associated with applying the defense rather than merely observing the attacked model under the same setting.

controls.name: Oracle filtering condition
controls.detail: For training-time defense, the paper reports an oracle that removes all poisoned samples and retains all normal samples.
controls.rules_out: Provides an upper-bound reference for the effect of perfect poisoned-sample removal.

confounds.name: Poisoned inputs may be adversarial or semantically changed rather than demonstrating a backdoor effect
confounds.detail: ASR could be high because the poisoned sample itself perturbs the model or changes meaning, even without an injected backdoor.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Reports ASR at poison rate 0 as a check for adversarial samples and reports USE similarity between clean and poisoned inputs to assess semantic preservation.

confounds.name: Low ASR under defense could come from rejecting clean inputs and damaging model utility
confounds.detail: A defense that rejects many inputs, including benign ones, can lower attack success without selectively identifying poisoned samples.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Reports clean accuracy and, for inference-time detection, FAR and FRR; the paper specifically notes that RAP rejects many clean samples and damages utility.

evidence_standards.name: Five random runs for selected results
evidence_standards.detail: Scenario I stealthiness and validity scores are averaged over five random runs; Scenario II attack effectiveness is averaged over five runs because it fluctuates substantially. The paper reports no error bars in its checklist and specifies no statistical test or significance threshold.

confounds.name: The apparent defense may depend on attackers not adapting training to evade GradCAM
confounds.detail: An adaptive attacker could train the Trojaned model to reduce GradCAM salience on Trojaned inputs, potentially undermining the removal mechanism.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper varies the GradCAM-evasion loss penalization and measures classification accuracy, attack success rate, and prediction confidence; it reports that stronger evasion degrades attack success and/or model accuracy and reduces confidence.

confounds.name: Large triggers may make restoration damage classification performance even when the attack is blocked
confounds.detail: Removing and restoring a large portion of an image can lower accuracy, so low ASR alone could overstate the defense’s practical success.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper measures attack success rate and classification accuracy as trigger size increases, reporting that for triggers covering 25% of GTSRB images ASR is 1.93% while accuracy falls to 80.61%.

confounds.name: Partial backdoors may remain effective after sanitization, or suppressing them may trade off classification accuracy
confounds.detail: For a source-label-specific attack, Februus may not fully neutralize the trigger; stronger mitigation could come at the cost of model performance.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For the partial-backdoor experiment, the paper reports ASR falling from 97.95% to 15.24%, and reports classification accuracy on sanitized Trojaned inputs and benign inputs (83.61% and 89.60%, respectively).

metrics.name: Attack success rate (ASR)
metrics.caveat: ASR alone does not capture confidence in successful target-class predictions; the paper also reports TMC.

metrics.name: Trojan misclassification confidence (TMC)
metrics.caveat: Complements ASR by measuring target-class confidence on successful trigger attacks; for attacks with equal ASR, the paper treats higher TMC as stronger.

metrics.name: Clean accuracy drop (CAD), attack-performance definition
metrics.caveat: Measures the clean-accuracy difference between benign and trojan models; the paper also uses CCC to measure clean-input confidence.

metrics.name: Clean classification confidence (CCC)
metrics.caveat: Complements attack-performance CAD by measuring confidence assigned to ground-truth classes of clean inputs.

metrics.name: Efficacy-specificity AUC (AUC)
metrics.caveat: Aggregates the ASR-CAD trade-off and can obscure its shape; the paper also plots the ASR-CAD trade-off, and interprets smaller AUC as a stronger leverage effect.

metrics.name: Attack rate deduction (ARD)
metrics.caveat: Measures the change in ASR after a defense; the paper also reports TMC to show the defense's effect on trigger-input confidence.

metrics.name: Clean accuracy drop (CAD), defense-utility definition
metrics.caveat: Measures the clean-accuracy difference before and after defense; the paper also reports CCC for clean-input confidence.

metrics.name: True positive rate (TPR)
metrics.caveat: For input filtering, TPR alone omits clean-input false alarms; the paper reports FPR and fixes it at 0.05 in the Strip/Neo comparison.

metrics.name: False positive rate (FPR)
metrics.caveat: Reported alongside TPR; the Strip/Neo comparison fixes FPR at 0.05.

metrics.name: Anomaly index value (AIV)
metrics.caveat: Model-inspection scores are interpreted relative to other classes; the paper uses the largest AIV on clean models to measure false positives and notes that AIV above 2 corresponds to over 95% probability of an anomaly.

metrics.name: Mask L1 norm (MLN)
metrics.caveat: Does not by itself show overlap with the injected trigger; the paper reports MJS alongside it.

metrics.name: Mask Jaccard similarity (MJS)
metrics.caveat: Measures mask overlap, not recovered-trigger size; the paper reports MLN alongside it.

metrics.name: Average running time (ART)
metrics.caveat: The paper measures it per model for offline sanitization/inspection and per input for online filtering/reformation.

controls.name: No-defense (vanilla) condition
controls.detail: Defense results are compared with the attack's no-defense result; the paper also uses vanilla as the reference for defense impact on clean accuracy.
controls.rules_out: That the reported defense effect is merely the attack's performance without applying a defense.

controls.name: Clean benign model without attack or defense
controls.detail: Used as the clean-accuracy reference in defense utility results and as the clean-model reference in model-inspection false-positive measurement.
controls.rules_out: That observed accuracy changes or model-inspection anomalies are present in the unmodified clean reference condition.

controls.name: Non-adaptive Imc
controls.detail: Compared with Imc adapted to Mp, Ar, Strip, and Abs.
controls.rules_out: That the adaptive attack's result is explained by using Imc without defense-specific adaptation.

controls.name: Benign-model retraining condition
controls.detail: Compared with training the trojan model from scratch, with ASR and CAD reported for both strategies.
controls.rules_out: That the reported training-from-scratch result is simply the outcome of using benign-model retraining.

confounds.name: Higher attack efficacy could come at the cost of greater clean-accuracy damage
confounds.detail: An attack could appear more effective because it damages clean performance more, rather than because its trigger attack is better.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For the trigger-size comparison, bound CAD for all attacks below 3% by controlling optimization iterations; in the single-pixel experiment, constrain CAD to at most 5%.

confounds.name: Input-filtering detection could look effective by flagging too many clean inputs
confounds.detail: A high TPR could result from an unacceptably high rate of clean inputs being classified as triggers.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report TPR at a fixed FPR of 0.05 for the Strip/Neo comparison.

confounds.name: Model-inspection detection could mistake clean models for trojan models
confounds.detail: An apparent detection result could reflect anomalous scores on clean models rather than identification of trojan models.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For clean models, use the largest class AIV to quantify the false-positive rate; report clean-model AIV results alongside trojan-model results.

confounds.name: Attribution-map detection may be vulnerable to an adaptive adversary
confounds.detail: The attribution-map differences could disappear if an adversary adapts the attack to deceive the interpretability-based detection.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out in the reported experiments; the authors state that whether an adversary can adapt to deceive such detection requires further study.

confounds.name: Results may depend on the particular model configuration or data split
confounds.detail: The measured attack/defense performance could change under other model configurations or train/test splits.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the authors acknowledge that they use popular DNN models and a fixed training/test split, and leave these effects for future study.

evidence_standards.name: 10 trojan models per attack setting and 100 clean-trigger input pairs per model
evidence_standards.detail: The paper says results are averaged over these cases across experiments.

evidence_standards.name: Standard deviation reporting
evidence_standards.detail: Several tables explicitly report standard deviations, including defense ARD/TMC and clean-accuracy results, input-filtering TPR, and model-inspection AIV.

evidence_standards.name: Fixed false-positive rate for input-filtering comparison
evidence_standards.detail: Strip and Neo TPR results are reported at FPR = 0.05.

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: 10 classes; 60,000 training and 10,000 testing grayscale 28×28 images. Trigger optimization uses the training set until convergence; classification accuracy and attack success rate are measured on test images, with the trigger applied for attack-success evaluation.

datasets.name: GTSRB
datasets.eval_protocol: 43 classes; the paper reports 35,288 training images in its task summary and 12,600 test images, with 32×32 color inputs. Trigger optimization uses the training set; classification accuracy and attack success rate are measured on test images.

datasets.name: YouTube Face
datasets.eval_protocol: 1,283 classes; preprocessing follows prior work, yielding 375,645 training and 64,200 testing images, with 55×47×3 inputs. Trigger optimization uses training images; test images are used for classification-accuracy and attack-success evaluation. For low-cost detection, the paper uses the top 100 labels during early iterations, then fully optimizes those labels and 100 randomly sampled labels.

datasets.name: PubFig
datasets.eval_protocol: 65 classes; 5,850 training and 650 testing color images at 224×224. The model uses transfer learning from a 16-layer VGG-Face teacher, fine-tuning its last four layers. Trigger optimization uses the training set; classification accuracy and attack success rate are measured on test images.

datasets.name: VGG-Face
datasets.eval_protocol: The Trojan Square and Trojan Watermark models recognize 2,622 people. The original dataset has 2.6 million images; because the original train/test split was unspecified, the authors randomly select 10,000 images as a test set.

baselines.name: Fine-Pruning
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper reports applying it to the GTSRB model and observing rapid model-performance degradation; no further comparison-matching details are stated.

metrics.name: attack success rate
metrics.caveat: For pruning, success on the reverse-engineered trigger can fail to reflect success on the attacker's original trigger, especially for Trojan models; the paper also measures attack success using the original trigger.

metrics.name: anomaly index
metrics.caveat: The paper interprets the threshold using an assumed normal distribution; it also checks clean models, whose anomaly indices are below the detection threshold.

metrics.name: L1 norm of trigger mask
metrics.caveat: A larger original trigger can make the reverse-engineered trigger's norm blend into the uninfected-label distribution and weaken outlier detection; the paper reports anomaly index alongside trigger norms.

metrics.name: false positive rate (FPR)
metrics.caveat: Reported alongside false negative rate (FNR) at selected FPR thresholds.

metrics.name: false negative rate (FNR)
metrics.caveat: Reported alongside FPR at selected FPR thresholds.

metrics.name: average neuron activation
metrics.caveat: The paper compares activations for clean inputs and inputs with both the reverse-engineered and original triggers, since the two triggers may produce different activation profiles.

metrics.name: number or ratio of neurons pruned
metrics.caveat: Pruning can also reduce clean classification accuracy; the paper reports classification accuracy alongside attack success rate.

controls.name: clean, uninfected model
controls.detail: For attack-injection experiments, the paper trains a clean model with the same training configuration but clean data; it also compares infected models with their matching original clean models.
controls.rules_out: That the detection result is simply an anomaly present in the corresponding clean model, and provides a clean-model reference for classification performance.

controls.name: unlearning with clean images only
controls.detail: Fine-tune using clean training images without adding the reverse-engineered trigger and without changing labels.
controls.rules_out: That unlearning works merely because of fine-tuning on clean data, without trigger-specific unlearning.

controls.name: unlearning with the original trigger
controls.detail: Use the same sampled training data as the reverse-trigger unlearning condition, but stamp the original trigger on the modified portion instead.
controls.rules_out: Whether the reported unlearning result depends on using the original trigger rather than the reverse-engineered trigger.

confounds.name: The apparent mitigation is general damage to clean-task capability, not backdoor removal
confounds.detail: Attack success could fall because pruning or fine-tuning damages the classifier generally, making the headline reduction in attack success misleading.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure clean classification accuracy alongside attack success rate after pruning and unlearning.

confounds.name: The reverse-engineered trigger is not representative of the attacker's original trigger
confounds.detail: A defense that succeeds only against the inferred trigger may appear effective while leaving the actual attack trigger effective; the paper notes this mismatch is especially consequential for Trojan models.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate attack success using the original trigger as well as the reverse-engineered trigger, and compare neuron activations for clean inputs and inputs carrying each trigger.

confounds.name: A naturally vulnerable label in a clean model is mistaken for an infected target
confounds.detail: A small trigger norm or outlier score could reflect ordinary label vulnerability rather than a backdoor.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate matching clean models as well as infected models and compare their anomaly indices; the reported clean models remain below the detection threshold.

confounds.name: A large trigger can blend into the uninfected-label trigger-norm distribution
confounds.detail: If the inferred trigger is no longer an outlier, the detector may miss a backdoor despite the attack being present.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Vary trigger size on GTSRB and measure trigger norms and anomaly index; the paper reports that detection can fail when the trigger exceeds 14×14 pixels.

confounds.name: Multiple infected labels can dilute the outlier signal
confounds.detail: Several backdoors may make individual infected-label trigger norms less exceptional, undermining the outlier-based detection claim.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Vary the number of infected labels and measure anomaly index and attack success; the paper reports that detection becomes difficult above 8 infected GTSRB labels.

confounds.name: A source-label-specific backdoor is missed by a detector designed for arbitrary source labels
confounds.detail: A partial backdoor may only affect a subset of source classes, so the standard all-input optimization can fail to expose it.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Modify detection to optimize over source–target label pairs and test it on an MNIST source–target backdoor; the authors note the added computation cost.

evidence_standards.name: MAD outlier rule: anomaly index greater than 2
evidence_standards.detail: The paper treats scores above 2 as outliers, stating this corresponds to greater than 95% probability under a normal-distribution assumption; it examines only low-end trigger-norm outliers as infected.

evidence_standards.name: Trigger-optimization success threshold greater than 99%
evidence_standards.detail: The optimization adjusts λ dynamically to obtain more than 99% successful misclassification of clean images into the candidate target label.

evidence_standards.name: Repeated robustness experiments
evidence_standards.detail: Some trigger-size and multiple-infected-label results are averaged over 10 rounds. The paper does not state a general seed count, confidence-interval rule, or statistical test for deciding whether differences are real.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: 10 classes, 5,000 training images and 1,000 test images per class (32×32×3). Reports benign accuracy (correct predictions on the benign test set) and attack success rate (triggered test samples classified as the target); the main setting uses a 1% poisoning rate and target class 0. Uses random crop and random horizontal flip for training augmentation. Also evaluates other poisoning rates, target labels, trigger constraints, limited training-data subsets, all-to-all and clean-label settings.

datasets.name: VGGFace2
datasets.eval_protocol: A constructed 20-class subset, with 400 training images and 100 test images per class (128×128×3). Reports benign accuracy on the benign test set and attack success rate on triggered test samples; the main setting uses a 1% poisoning rate and target class 0. Uses random crop and random horizontal flip for training augmentation.

baselines.fair_comparison: Compared under the shared 1% poisoning rate, target class 0, victim architectures, and victim training configurations; uses a 3×3 checkerboard on CIFAR-10 and a 20×20 white patch on VGGFace2.

baselines.fair_comparison: Compared under the shared 1% poisoning rate, target class 0, victim architectures, and victim training configurations; uses transparency 0.2, with a Hello-Kitty trigger on CIFAR-10 and random-noise trigger on VGGFace2.

baselines.fair_comparison: Compared under the shared 1% poisoning rate, target class 0, victim architectures, and victim training configurations; uses a pre-trained model to generate the targeted universal adversarial perturbation, with L-infinity constraint 8/255 on both datasets.

baselines.name: WaNet

metrics.caveat: For Scale-Up, the paper also reports TPR, FPR, and ASR; it judges detection unsatisfactory despite the reported detection measures because average ASR remains above 70%.

metrics.name: Neural Cleanse anomaly index
metrics.caveat: Compared with the threshold of 2; the paper reports the index alongside that threshold.

metrics.name: MNTD trojan score
metrics.caveat: The paper also reports AUROC (0.57) for the scores.

metrics.name: Human image-selection accuracy

controls.name: No Attack
controls.detail: A model trained without attack, reported alongside attacked models.
controls.rules_out: That the reported benign accuracy of attacked models is being interpreted without a clean-model reference.

controls.name: Random
controls.detail: A random-noise trigger constrained to have the same L-infinity and L-zero budgets as SIBA.
controls.rules_out: That the attack result follows merely from using a sparse, low-magnitude trigger with those budgets.

controls.name: Sparse

controls.rules_out: That magnitude optimization alone, without SIBA's trigger optimization, explains the result.

confounds.name: SIBA's performance depends on access to the whole training set
confounds.detail: The main trigger optimization uses the whole training set, so the result might rely on unusually extensive adversary data access.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Optimizes triggers using subsets from 5% to 20% of CIFAR-10 training data and reports victim BA and ASR; reports over 90% ASR at 10% data.

confounds.name: SIBA's performance depends on knowing the victim model architecture
confounds.detail: The main experiments use the same architecture for the surrogate and victim, which may not be feasible when the victim architecture is unknown.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluates cross-architecture transfer on CIFAR-10 using ResNet18, ResNet34, VGG16, and VGG19 as surrogate and victim structures.

confounds.name: Perceptual metrics do not establish that people cannot see the trigger
confounds.detail: The reported image-distance measures could fail to capture whether human observers can identify poisoned images.
confounds.ruled_out_by: A survey with 20 participants asks them to select the modified image among four clean images and one SIBA-poisoned image per set; reports 23% selection accuracy.

evidence_standards.name: Human stealthiness survey
evidence_standards.detail: 20 participants; each survey has five sets, with four clean images and one SIBA-poisoned image per set. The paper treats 23% overall selection accuracy as close to the 20% random-guess rate.

metrics.name: Attack Success Rate (ASR)
metrics.caveat: A lower ASR can accompany substantial loss of clean-data accuracy; the paper reports accuracy alongside ASR and discusses their trade-off.

metrics.name: Accuracy (Acc)
metrics.caveat: Accuracy alone does not show whether triggered inputs still reach the attacker’s target label; the paper reports ASR alongside accuracy.

controls.name: Unmodified backdoored model (“Before”)
controls.detail: The tables report ASR and accuracy before any defense is applied.
controls.rules_out: Provides a reference for whether the defense changes the backdoored model’s measured ASR and accuracy.

controls.name: BaEraser with the penalty term nearly canceled
controls.detail: The paper varies β/α; at a very small ratio the penalty is approximately canceled, allowing comparison with settings where it has more influence.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the dynamic penalty helps limit accuracy loss and catastrophic forgetting rather than the result coming from unlearning alone.

controls.name: Correct-label target condition
controls.detail: The paper examines an attacker condition in which the target label is already the correct label for the input.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether unlearning indiscriminately removes correct memories; the authors report that the penalty restrains this effect.

confounds.name: Lower ASR is caused by general model damage or catastrophic forgetting, rather than selective backdoor removal
confounds.detail: The headline ASR reduction could also occur if unlearning damaged the model’s performance on clean inputs.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure clean-data accuracy alongside ASR, examine their trade-off during unlearning, and report that BaEraser lowers ASR with less than 5% average accuracy drop in the stated comparison.

confounds.name: Recovered triggers are adversarial noises rather than valid backdoor trigger patterns
confounds.detail: If recovered patterns only fool individual inputs, successful unlearning on them would not establish recovery of the backdoor trigger distribution.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate recovered patterns across a batch and retain patterns only when their attack success rate exceeds the threshold; the paper distinguishes this batch effect from adversarial examples affecting only an individual input.

confounds.name: Recovered patterns are invalid or do not correspond sufficiently to the injected triggers
confounds.detail: If recovery fails, the subsequent unlearning may not be removing the backdoor trigger memory as claimed.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Visualize original and recovered triggers and compare their patterns; the authors report that most-pixel differences are negligible, while acknowledging room for improvement.

evidence_standards.name: 5 random trials
evidence_standards.detail: All experimental results are averaged over 5 random trials; the paper does not specify variance estimates, confidence intervals, or statistical tests.

metrics.name: Attack success rate (ASR)
metrics.caveat: ASR alone does not capture attack specificity or confidence; the paper also reports CAD and TMC.

metrics.name: Trojan misclassification confidence (TMC)
metrics.caveat: Complements ASR by measuring target-class confidence on successful trigger attacks; for equal ASR, the paper treats higher TMC as stronger.

metrics.name: Clean accuracy drop (CAD)
metrics.caveat: For attack evaluation it measures clean-accuracy difference between benign and trojan models; for defense evaluation it is defined differently, as clean-accuracy change after defense. The paper also uses CCC to complement the clean-input assessment.

metrics.name: Clean classification confidence (CCC)
metrics.caveat: Complements CAD by measuring confidence assigned to ground-truth classes of clean inputs.

metrics.name: Efficacy-specificity AUC (AUC)
metrics.caveat: Aggregates the ASR-CAD trade-off; smaller AUC indicates a stronger leverage effect in the paper's interpretation.

metrics.name: Neuron-separation ratio (NSR)
metrics.caveat: Measures separation of top-k active neurons for clean and trigger inputs; it compares activation patterns, rather than directly measuring attack success.

metrics.name: Attack rate deduction (ARD)
metrics.caveat: Measures the change in ASR after defense; the paper also reports TMC to show the defense's effect on trigger-input confidence and CAD for clean utility.

metrics.name: True positive rate (TPR)
metrics.caveat: For input filtering, detection accuracy depends on false positives; the paper reports TPR at fixed FPR = 0.05.

metrics.name: False positive rate (FPR)
metrics.caveat: Measures clean inputs incorrectly detected as triggers; reported alongside TPR, with FPR fixed at 0.05 in the Strip/Neo comparison.

metrics.name: Anomaly index value (AIV)
metrics.caveat: For model inspection, the paper uses the target-class AIV for trojan models and the largest class AIV for clean models; AIV above 2 is described as having over 95% probability of being anomalous.

metrics.name: Mask L1 norm (MLN)
metrics.caveat: Trigger size alone does not show whether the recovered mask matches the injected trigger; the paper reports MJS alongside MLN.

metrics.name: Mask Jaccard similarity (MJS)
metrics.caveat: Measures overlap of recovered and injected trigger masks; it is undefined for Tb because trigger position is random.

metrics.name: Average running time (ART)
metrics.caveat: The timing unit depends on whether the defense runs offline or online: per model for sanitization/inspection, per input for filtering/reformation.

controls.name: Vanilla/no-defense reference
controls.detail: Defense results are compared with the no-defense case; clean-accuracy results also use the clean model without attack or defense as a reference.
controls.rules_out: That measured changes are simply the attack or defense setting's reference-level behavior rather than an effect associated with applying the defense.

controls.name: Benign-model reference
controls.detail: For attack comparisons, benign-model accuracy is used to calculate CAD; benign models are also compared with trojan models for NSR and attribution-map analyses.
controls.rules_out: That the observed clean-accuracy, neuron-activation, or attribution differences are present in the unmodified model as well.

controls.name: Non-adaptive Imc
controls.detail: The defense-adapted Imc variants are compared with non-adaptive Imc against Mp, Ar, Strip, and Abs.
controls.rules_out: That the adaptive-attack results follow merely from using Imc rather than adapting it to the defense.

controls.name: Regular trigger
controls.detail: Random-position triggers with the same number of pixels are compared with regular-shaped triggers.
controls.rules_out: That the reported difference is due only to trigger size rather than relaxing the spatial constraint.

controls.name: Benign-model retraining
controls.detail: Training trojan models from scratch is compared with retraining benign models, with ASR and CAD reported for both.
controls.rules_out: That the training-from-scratch result is attributable merely to allowing a different clean-accuracy change.

controls.name: Standard Imc backpropagation
controls.detail: Imc with reduced skip-connection gradients is compared with normal training.
controls.rules_out: That any ASR change is due merely to using the modified backpropagation procedure rather than the gradient adjustment being tested.

confounds.name: Higher ASR could come from sacrificing clean accuracy
confounds.detail: An attack might appear more effective simply because it damages performance on clean inputs.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper bounds CAD below 3% in the trigger-size comparison and below 5% for the single-pixel experiment; it also reports CAD alongside ASR in attack trade-off experiments.

confounds.name: Defense robustness could come from damaging clean utility
confounds.detail: A defense might reduce attack success by broadly degrading classification rather than selectively mitigating the backdoor.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports clean-input CAD alongside ARD and TMC for attack-agnostic defenses.

confounds.name: Architecture-specific behavior could explain attack differences
confounds.detail: An attack result on one network might reflect that model's individual architecture rather than a broader pattern.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper evaluates VGG, ResNet, and DenseNet, stating that distinct architectures are used to factor out individual model characteristics.

confounds.name: Attribution-map differences could reflect class-related differences rather than a backdoor
confounds.detail: Clean and trigger inputs can be evaluated with respect to different classes, so a map difference alone might not indicate a trojan effect.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares attribution-map distances for original and target classes on both benign and trojan models; the reported target-class distance is much larger for the trojan model.

evidence_standards.name: 10 generated trojan models and 100 clean-trigger pairs per model; results averaged
evidence_standards.detail: The paper states this as its general experimental protocol. It reports standard deviations in several result tables, but specifies no inferential statistical test or significance threshold.

evidence_standards.name: 100 clean-trigger pairs per attack; TPR at FPR = 0.05
evidence_standards.detail: Used for the Strip/Neo detection comparison; standard deviations are reported. No statistical test or decision threshold for declaring a difference real is specified.

datasets.name: SST-2
datasets.eval_protocol: Train/test split: 6,920/1,821. Evaluate attack success rate (ASR) on triggered test examples and clean accuracy (CACC) on clean test data; sentiment target is positive. Results are averaged over three random seeds. For LLMBkd and StyleBkd poison data, manually match SST-2’s original formatting (including tokenization-related spacing and capitalization).

datasets.name: HSOL
datasets.eval_protocol: Train/test split: 5,823/2,485. Evaluate ASR on triggered test examples and CACC on clean test data; the abuse-detection target is non-toxic. Results are averaged over three random seeds.

datasets.name: ToxiGen
datasets.eval_protocol: Train/test split: 7,168/896. Evaluate ASR on triggered test examples and CACC on clean test data; the abuse-detection target is non-toxic. Results are averaged over three random seeds.

datasets.name: AG News
datasets.eval_protocol: Train/test split: 108,000/7,600. Evaluate ASR on triggered test examples and CACC on clean test data; the topic-classification target is world. Results are averaged over three random seeds.

baselines.name: Addsent
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same datasets with the same RoBERTa victim model and poisoning-rate settings; compared with and without poison selection in the corresponding black-box and gray-box settings.

baselines.name: BadNets
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same datasets with the same RoBERTa victim model and poisoning-rate settings; compared with and without poison selection in the corresponding black-box and gray-box settings.

baselines.name: StyleBkd
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same datasets with the same RoBERTa victim model and poisoning-rate settings; Bible style is used unless specified. Direct style comparisons use matching styles for StyleBkd and LLMBkd, and poison selection is compared consistently across gray-box and black-box settings.

baselines.name: SynBkd
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same datasets with the same RoBERTa victim model and poisoning-rate settings; compared with and without poison selection in the corresponding black-box and gray-box settings.

baselines.name: BKI
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same backdoored models and datasets, using 1% poison data and gray-box poison selection for the attacks.

baselines.name: CUBE
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same backdoored models and datasets, using 1% poison data and gray-box poison selection for the attacks.

baselines.name: ONION
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same backdoored models and datasets, using 1% poison data and gray-box poison selection for the attacks.

baselines.name: RAP
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same backdoored models and datasets, using 1% poison data and gray-box poison selection for the attacks.

baselines.name: STRIP
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same backdoored models and datasets, using 1% poison data and gray-box poison selection for the attacks.

metrics.name: Perplexity (PPL) increase
metrics.caveat: Lower PPL is taken as indicating more natural text, but the authors caution that text that scores as natural by PPL may still be unnatural in the context of the original dataset; they also report grammar errors, USE, and MAUVE.

metrics.name: Grammar error (GE) increase
metrics.caveat: Lower GE is taken as indicating more natural text, but the authors caution that text that scores as natural by grammar errors may still be unnatural in the context of the original dataset; they also report PPL, USE, and MAUVE.

metrics.name: Human label error rate
metrics.caveat: The authors report that Amazon Mechanical Turk results barely exceeded chance even on original SST-2 labels, so they instead use five unaffiliated graduate-student annotators and majority vote.

controls.name: Poison selection ablation
controls.detail: Run attacks both with poison examples selected by a clean model and without poison selection.
controls.rules_out: That the reported attack improvement is simply due to using the attack method, rather than the paper’s poison-selection technique.

controls.name: No-defense reference
controls.detail: Report attack success rate on backdoored models without applying a defense, alongside models after each defense.
controls.rules_out: That a change in attack success rate is present without applying the defense.

confounds.name: Poison examples may not actually preserve their labels
confounds.detail: The apparent clean-label attack results could instead depend on generated poison texts whose content does not match their assigned target labels.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Human evaluation on SST-2: five unaffiliated graduate students labeled the same 600 instances, balanced between positive and negative sentiment; final labels use majority vote, and label error rates are reported for original and poisoned examples.

confounds.name: Formatting artifacts, rather than style, could drive learning
confounds.detail: SST-2’s unusual capitalization, spacing, and tokenization formats could provide noisy signals that affect model learning independently of the trigger style.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Manually modify LLMBkd and StyleBkd poison texts to match the original SST-2 formatting.

confounds.name: The attack could damage general clean performance rather than selectively trigger target predictions
confounds.detail: High ASR could arise from broadly degraded classifier performance rather than a learned backdoor response to triggered inputs.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure and report CACC on clean test data alongside ASR.

confounds.name: Measured text naturalness may not reflect naturalness in the dataset context
confounds.detail: A trigger can appear natural by perplexity or grammar-error measures while still being unnatural in the context of the original dataset; the authors explicitly note this limitation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the authors acknowledge this limitation; they report PPL, grammar errors, USE, and MAUVE, but state these do not settle contextual naturalness.

evidence_standards.name: Three random seeds
evidence_standards.detail: Results are averaged over three random seeds. The paper does not specify variance estimates, confidence intervals, or a statistical significance test.

evidence_standards.name: Human evaluation: five annotators and majority vote
evidence_standards.detail: Five unaffiliated computer-science graduate students each labeled the same 600 SST-2 instances, evenly split between positive and negative sentiment; majority vote determines the final human label.

datasets.name: SST-2
datasets.eval_protocol: Text classification; report clean-test accuracy (Acc) and attack success rate (ASR) on trigger-embedded test samples. Training data are generated with OpenBackdoor; poison rates are 5% for BadNet and InsertSent, and 20% for syntactic and multi-type attacks. No split sizes or test counts are specified. Also evaluated with Llama-2-7B for BadNet, InsertSent, syntactic, and multi-type attacks.

datasets.name: OffensEval
datasets.eval_protocol: Offensive-language classification; report clean-test accuracy (Acc) and attack success rate (ASR) on trigger-embedded test samples. Training data are generated with OpenBackdoor; poison rates are 5% for BadNet and InsertSent, and 20% for syntactic and multi-type attacks. No split sizes or test counts are specified. Also evaluated with Llama-2-7B for BadNet, InsertSent, syntactic, and multi-type attacks.

datasets.name: AG News
datasets.eval_protocol: Four-class news-topic classification; report clean-test accuracy (Acc) and attack success rate (ASR) on trigger-embedded test samples. Training data are generated with OpenBackdoor; poison rates are 5% for BadNet and InsertSent, and 20% for syntactic and multi-type attacks. No split sizes or test counts are specified.

baselines.name: ONION
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same tasks and attack settings; the paper runs the open-source code by Qi et al. (2021a).

baselines.name: BKI
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same tasks and attack settings; re-implemented based on OpenBackdoor.

baselines.name: STRIP
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same tasks and attack settings; re-implemented based on OpenBackdoor.

baselines.name: RAP
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same tasks and attack settings; re-implemented based on OpenBackdoor.

baselines.name: NoDefense
baselines.fair_comparison: Reference condition: vanilla BERT-base fine-tuned on poisoned data without defense; the paper says it is not directly comparable with defense results.

baselines.name: Benign
baselines.fair_comparison: Reference condition: model trained on clean data without poisoned samples; the paper says it is not directly comparable with defense results.

controls.name: PoE without denoising
controls.detail: The paper compares DPoE with PoE alone, omitting the denoising module.
controls.rules_out: A difference in clean accuracy or defense performance supports a contribution from adding denoising to the PoE framework.

controls.name: NoDefense
controls.detail: A vanilla BERT-base model is fine-tuned on the poisoned data without defense.
controls.rules_out: Shows performance relative to training on the poisoned data without applying a defense.

confounds.name: Lower ASR could reflect general loss of model utility rather than effective defense
confounds.detail: A defense might reduce attack success simply by damaging performance more broadly.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report clean-test accuracy alongside ASR to measure utility on benign data.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates poisoned models using clean accuracy (ACC) on clean samples and attack success rate (ASR) on triggered samples. Uses BadNets (3×3 checkerboard; clean-label; 0.5% poison rate), LC (0.5%), Blended with Hello-Kitty trigger (5%), and WaNet (5%); class 2 is the target. Trains ResNet-18 for 100 epochs with random crop and random horizontal flip. The test split and its size are not specified.

datasets.name: CIFAR-100
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates poisoned models using ACC on clean samples and ASR on triggered samples, across the backdoor attacks considered in the paper. The paper says settings are similar to CIFAR-10 and leaves CIFAR-100 details to Appendix A; the test split and its size are not specified.

baselines.name: Fine Pruning (FP)
baselines.fair_comparison: Grid-searched pruning ratio from 5% to 95% in steps of 5%; selected the result whose clean accuracy was closest to CAT’s.

baselines.name: Neural Attention Distillation (NAD)
baselines.fair_comparison: Followed the original settings, except the initial learning rate was set to 0.01 for more stable results.

baselines.name: Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DPSGD)
baselines.fair_comparison: Replaced batch normalization with group normalization and set the noise level σ to 0.1.

baselines.name: Anti-Backdoor Learning (ABL)
baselines.fair_comparison: Used the settings in ABL’s paper except for the loss threshold γ, set to 0 for a better detection rate.

metrics.name: Clean accuracy (ACC)
metrics.caveat: AT can reduce clean accuracy; the paper reports ACC alongside ASR to show the clean-accuracy cost of backdoor robustness.

metrics.name: Attack success rate (ASR)
metrics.caveat: ASR alone does not show the clean-accuracy cost; the paper reports ACC alongside it.

controls.name: Random input perturbations
controls.detail: Compared adversarial training with models trained using random perturbations. For BadNets, random spatial transformations were used; for Blended attacks, zero-mean Gaussian noise was added. The paper highlights a comparison at similar clean accuracy (about 84%) for BadNets.
controls.rules_out: That random input perturbation, rather than adversarially selected perturbations, explains the backdoor mitigation.

controls.name: No defense
controls.detail: Reports ACC and ASR for models trained without a backdoor defense alongside the defense results.
controls.rules_out: Provides an unmodified reference for judging whether the defense changes ACC or ASR.

controls.name: Single-perturbation AT
controls.detail: Compared CAT with AT using only one perturbation, including L∞ AT alone and Spatial AT alone.
controls.rules_out: That CAT’s results follow merely from using one of its perturbations rather than combining them.

controls.name: Alternative AT combinations
controls.detail: Compared CAT with L2+Spatial, Perceptual+Spatial, and L∞+Perceptual combinations.
controls.rules_out: That the reported results are explained by combining arbitrary AT perturbations rather than CAT’s chosen combination.

confounds.name: Random perturbations, rather than adversarial perturbations, account for backdoor mitigation
confounds.detail: The headline robustness might arise from perturbing training inputs generally, without adversarial perturbations being responsible.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compared random-perturbation training with adversarial training; for BadNets, spatial AT achieved ASR below 5% while a randomly perturbed model at similar clean accuracy had ASR 44.98%. The paper also reports random-perturbation comparisons for Blended attacks.

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: All-to-one attack; reports clean, predefined-warp attack, and random-warp noise-mode accuracy. Uses 60,000 training images, 10 classes, and 28×28×1 inputs; test split and test-set size are not specified.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: All-to-one attack; reports clean, predefined-warp attack, and random-warp noise-mode accuracy. Uses 50,000 training images, 10 classes, and 32×32×3 inputs; test split and test-set size are not specified.

datasets.name: GTSRB
datasets.eval_protocol: All-to-one attack; reports clean, predefined-warp attack, and random-warp noise-mode accuracy. Uses 39,252 training images, 43 classes, and 32×32×3 inputs; test split and test-set size are not specified. For human inspection, 25 images were selected, each method's 25 generated backdoor images were mixed with the originals, and participants judged whether each image was genuine.

datasets.name: CelebA
datasets.eval_protocol: All-to-one attack; reports clean, predefined-warp attack, and random-warp noise-mode accuracy. Selects the three most balanced attributes—Heavy Makeup, Mouth Slightly Open, and Smiling—and concatenates them into eight classes. Uses 202,599 training images and 64×64×3 inputs; test split and test-set size are not specified.

baselines.name: Patched
baselines.fair_comparison: In the human inspection study, compared using the same 25 selected GTSRB images, corresponding original/backdoor image sets, and participants as the other methods.

baselines.name: Blended
baselines.fair_comparison: In the human inspection study, compared using the same 25 selected GTSRB images, corresponding original/backdoor image sets, and participants as the other methods.

baselines.name: SIG
baselines.fair_comparison: In the human inspection study, compared using the same 25 selected GTSRB images, corresponding original/backdoor image sets, and participants as the other methods.

baselines.name: ReFool
baselines.fair_comparison: In the human inspection study, compared using the same 25 selected GTSRB images, corresponding original/backdoor image sets, and participants as the other methods.

metrics.name: Human inspection success fooling rate
metrics.caveat: The paper says the rate can be higher on both clean and backdoor inputs when the two are harder to distinguish; it reports rates separately for backdoor inputs, clean inputs, and all inputs.

controls.name: Clean mode
controls.detail: Inputs are left unwarped and retain their correct labels; clean-mode accuracy is reported alongside attack-mode accuracy.
controls.rules_out: Shows whether the model's attack-mode behavior comes with a loss of ordinary clean-input classification performance.

controls.name: Noise mode
controls.detail: Inputs receive a random warping field different from the predefined backdoor field and retain their correct labels; noise-mode accuracy is reported alongside clean- and attack-mode accuracy.
controls.rules_out: Shows that the model responds to the predefined warp rather than treating arbitrary warped inputs as backdoor triggers.

controls.name: Training without the noise mode
controls.detail: An ablation trains the backdoor model without the paper's noise-mode training condition and compares Neural Cleanse trigger patterns and detection results.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the noise-mode mechanism, rather than merely training a warped-trigger backdoor, accounts for avoiding the Neural Cleanse detection behavior.

confounds.name: The model learns pixel-wise artifacts instead of the intended warping trigger
confounds.detail: A successful attack could be attributed to artifacts in the poisoned training images rather than learning the predefined warp.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Tests the model on random warping and reports noise-mode accuracy; also compares Neural Cleanse patterns for models trained with and without noise mode. The paper reports that the noise-mode model retains correct-class accuracy on random warps and has a pattern like the clean model's.

confounds.name: The human-inspection fooling rate reflects clean-image judgments rather than stealth of backdoor images
confounds.detail: The overall rate could be high without testers having difficulty identifying the backdoor examples specifically.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Reports fooling rates separately: 38.6% for backdoor inputs, 17.4% for clean inputs, and 28.0% overall; it also discusses detected atypical warped examples as a limitation.

evidence_standards.name: Human inspection study size and procedure
evidence_standards.detail: 40 participants, trained about the attack mechanism and characteristics, judged 50 images per method (25 originals and 25 corresponding backdoor images), yielding 2,000 answers per method. No statistical test or uncertainty interval is reported.

evidence_standards.name: Physical recapture test size
evidence_standards.detail: 50 clean and 50 backdoor images were displayed on a screen and recaptured with a phone camera. The paper reports clean accuracy and attack success rate but no repeated runs, uncertainty interval, or statistical test.

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: BadNets single-target attack; 10 output labels with target 5, 28×28×1 inputs, 4×4 trigger (about 1%); about 10% manipulated training data. Detection experiments were repeated 10 times and average metrics reported. The paper does not specify the evaluation split.

datasets.name: GTSRB
datasets.eval_protocol: BadNets single-target attack; 43 output labels with target 18, 32×32×3 inputs, 4×4 trigger (about 1%); about 10% manipulated training data. Detection experiments were repeated 10 times and average metrics reported. The paper does not specify the evaluation split.

datasets.name: ResNet-18
datasets.eval_protocol: TrojanNN watermark-trigger benchmark; 1,000 labels with target 500, 224×224×3 inputs, 40×40 trigger (about 3%); the table reports top-5 test accuracy. Detection experiments were repeated 10 times and average metrics reported. The paper does not specify the evaluation split.

datasets.name: Trojan Square
datasets.eval_protocol: TrojanNN square-trigger benchmark on VGGFace 2; 2,622 labels with target 0, 224×224×3 inputs, trigger size about 3,512 pixels (7%). Detection experiments were repeated 10 times and average metrics reported. The paper does not specify the evaluation split.

datasets.name: Trojan WM
datasets.eval_protocol: TrojanNN watermark-trigger benchmark on VGGFace 2; 2,622 labels with target 0, 224×224×3 inputs, trigger size about 3,512 pixels (7%). Detection experiments were repeated 10 times and average metrics reported. The paper does not specify the evaluation split.

baselines.name: Neural Cleanse (NC)
baselines.fair_comparison: They use NC's open-source code and run it on the same model-inversion dataset obtained with the same model-inversion procedure as DeepInspect; runtime comparisons use an Nvidia RTX 2080 GPU with 8 GiB memory and recover 5 images per class during model inversion.

metrics.name: Deviation factor (df)
metrics.caveat: The stated significance interpretation assumes normally distributed perturbation statistics; the paper uses DMAD to estimate dispersion and compares df with cutoff c=2 (significance level α=0.05).

metrics.name: Test accuracy
metrics.caveat: The paper says stealthy backdoors are hard to identify using test accuracy as the detection criterion; it reports Trojan activation rate and trigger-based detection statistics alongside test accuracy.

metrics.name: Trigger perturbation level (DeepInspect soft-hinge loss on the l1 norm)
metrics.caveat: Trigger size affects detection statistics; the paper tests different square-trigger sizes and reports DeepInspect as less sensitive to increasing trigger size than NC.

metrics.name: l1 norm of recovered trigger (Neural Cleanse statistic)
metrics.caveat: The paper reports that NC's deviation factor decreases as trigger size increases and that NC has false negatives at some tested trigger sizes.

controls.name: Benign (uninfected) models
controls.detail: DeepInspect measures deviation factors on benign models alongside trojaned models across the benchmarks.
controls.rules_out: That the reported anomaly is simply present in the benign reference models under the same detection procedure.

confounds.name: Trigger size affects the detection statistic
confounds.detail: A detection result could depend on the chosen trigger size rather than hold across different trigger sizes; the paper notes trigger size affects both DeepInspect and NC statistics.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They vary square-trigger sizes on GTSRB and measure the methods' deviation factors; DeepInspect has no false negatives across the tested sizes, while NC has three.

confounds.name: Model patching suppresses TAR by damaging ordinary task performance
confounds.detail: A lower Trojan activation rate after patching could reflect general loss of model capability rather than mitigation of the backdoor.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They report test accuracy before and after patching alongside TAR; test accuracy is preserved on the reported benchmarks.

confounds.name: An adaptive attacker can avoid the small-perturbation anomaly
confounds.detail: The authors acknowledge that a white-box attacker could choose source and target classes so the required perturbation is not noticeably smaller than for unaffected classes, potentially lowering df.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out experimentally; the paper says this may reduce attack effectiveness and identifies it as a limitation.

evidence_standards.name: Repeated detection runs
evidence_standards.detail: Each Trojan detection experiment is repeated 10 times; the paper reports average metrics, without specifying a variance measure or statistical test across runs.

evidence_standards.name: DMAD anomaly cutoff
evidence_standards.detail: The paper uses cutoff c=2 for deviation factor, corresponding to significance level α=0.05 under its normal-distribution assumption; points above the cutoff are marked as outliers and their labels as suspicious attack targets.

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: For each of 144 configurations, train 15 models (2,160 total). Test on separate untriggered and triggered test subsets; poisoned examples are labeled 4 and relabeled 5. Aggregate classification results only for models meeting the paper’s 95% accuracy threshold on clean and triggered data.

datasets.name: Boxing-ram-v0
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate clean and triggered environments by average cumulative reward. During training, test about every 100K frames on 20 games per condition; measure final performance over 100 games per condition. The agent receives a four-step flat vector of simplified RAM features; the trigger adds 100 to observations modulo 256, and poisoned-environment rewards are multiplied by -1.

metrics.name: Clean test accuracy on triggered-label classes

controls.name: Untriggered clean test data
controls.detail: Evaluate the trained classifiers on test examples without the trigger, alongside triggered examples.
controls.rules_out: That triggered behavior is accompanied by loss of performance on normal inputs.

controls.name: Clean Boxing environment
controls.detail: Evaluate the agent in the unpoisoned environment, which behaves like Boxing-ram-v0 without the observation trigger or reward inversion.
controls.rules_out: That low reward in the poisoned environment reflects poor task performance generally rather than a trigger-conditioned effect.

evidence_standards.name: Classification: 15 trained models per configuration; 95% accuracy threshold
evidence_standards.detail: Generate 15 models for each configuration and compute aggregate statistics only for models passing the 95% clean-and-triggered accuracy threshold. Epoch counts are reported as mean ± standard deviation; the paper describes some triggered-accuracy results as statistically similar but specifies no statistical test.

evidence_standards.name: Reinforcement learning: repeated game evaluations
evidence_standards.detail: Intermediate evaluations use 20 games per condition about every 100K frames; final average cumulative rewards use 100 games per condition.

datasets.name: GTSRB
datasets.eval_protocol: 39,209 training and 12,603 test images are reported; the architecture table separately lists 35,288 as training size. Input size 32×32×3. The paper does not specify a further test-split scoring protocol.

datasets.name: YouTube Aligned Face (YouTube)
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses a filtered subset of about 375,645 images of 1,283 people; randomly selects 10 images per person as the test set. Input size 55×47×3.

datasets.name: Pubfig
datasets.eval_protocol: Reports 13,838 face images of 85 people; no evaluation split is specified. Input size 224×224×3.

datasets.name: ImageNet
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses ILSVRC 2012, reported as 1,281,167 training images across 1,000 classes; no evaluation split is specified. Input size 299×299×3.

datasets.name: Speech Digit (SD)
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses 5,000 English spoken-digit recordings, available as wav files and spectrum images; no evaluation split is specified. Input size 64×1.

baselines.name: BadNet
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same task datasets and target DNN architectures; uses the paper's stated BadNet configuration, including a poisoned subset of 20% of original training data and one target label. ImageNet baseline experiments are not reported.

baselines.name: TrojanAttack (TrojanAtk)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same task datasets and target DNN architectures; uses one target label and a subset of training data for the poisoned data, then fine-tunes the target model. The paper uses a training-data subset instead of TrojanAttack's generated dataset for time-saving. ImageNet baseline experiments are not reported.

metrics.name: Attack Accuracy (A_atk)
metrics.caveat: Attack accuracy alone does not measure whether the infected model stays silent on clean inputs; the paper evaluates denoising performance alongside it.

controls.name: Clean, unmodified model
controls.detail: The paper compares the clean model's anomaly index with those of BadNet-, TrojanAttack-, and TrojanNet-infected models, and uses pristine-model accuracy as the original-task reference.
controls.rules_out: A TrojanNet result being attributable merely to the clean model's baseline behavior; it provides a reference for detector scores and original-task accuracy.

confounds.name: TrojanNet may activate on clean or noisy inputs, rather than only on its trigger
confounds.detail: False-positive activations could undermine the claim that the infected model stays silent on ordinary inputs.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluates denoising on randomly selected patches from each application's test data; counts a prediction as correct only when every output-class probability is below 10^-4.

confounds.name: Attack performance may depend on the trigger's spatial position
confounds.detail: High attack accuracy at a selected position might not hold when the trigger is moved; the paper explicitly acknowledges spatial sensitivity for TrojanNet and prior methods.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper says it evaluates a method to mitigate position sensitivity in Sec. C; the supplied text does not include those results.

evidence_standards.name: Anomaly-index detection threshold
evidence_standards.detail: Following the cited prior-work settings, the paper classifies a model as infected when its anomaly index exceeds 2.0.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the 50,000 training images (10 classes, 5,000 per class); poisons 20, 75, 300, 1,250, or 5,000 examples from a target class. Attack success rate is measured on test examples not originally labeled as the target class, with the trigger applied; standard test accuracy is also reported. Some experiments use random left-right flips, random 2-pixel crops, and per-image standardization; others omit augmentation.

baselines.name: Gu et al. (2017) standard backdoor attack
Standard backdoor attack restricted to poisoning correctly labeled examples from the target class

metrics.name: Number of poisoned inputs among the highest-loss inspected inputs
Training loss on poisoned inputs
metrics.caveat: The paper reports median and interquartile range for poisoned inputs with and without the trigger, alongside average loss as a baseline.

controls.name: Gaussian noise added to poisoned inputs before the trigger
controls.detail: Adds zero-mean Gaussian noise at varying variances and measures attack performance.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether attack performance follows simply from adding noise or making inputs harder, rather than from preserving some salient input information while making classification difficult.

controls.name: Poisoned inputs evaluated without the backdoor trigger
controls.detail: Tracks their training loss without the trigger and compares it with loss when the trigger is present.
controls.rules_out: A lower loss with the trigger and persistently high loss without it supports reliance on the trigger rather than learning the poisoned inputs’ salient features.

controls.name: One-corner trigger with data augmentation
controls.detail: Compared with the four-corner trigger under data augmentation, and evaluated with and without augmentation.
controls.rules_out: Shows whether the four-corner trigger’s performance under augmentation is explained merely by applying augmentation.

confounds.name: Attack performance may come from generic corruption or difficulty rather than useful salient features in the poisoned inputs
confounds.detail: If merely making inputs noisy or hard to classify were sufficient, that could explain attack performance without the proposed account of preserving salient information while making classification difficult.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Adds zero-mean Gaussian noise at varying variances and measures attack success; low variance can help, while high variance harms performance.

confounds.name: The model may learn the poisoned inputs’ salient features rather than rely on the trigger
confounds.detail: If the model predicts the target from those features, attack success would not establish that the trigger is driving the prediction.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measures training loss on poisoned inputs with and without the trigger; loss remains high without the trigger while the model predicts correctly with it.

datasets.name: GTSRB
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the 39,209 training and 12,630 testing samples (43 classes; 32×32×3). Trains 6-Conv/2-MaxPooling models and, in the model-complexity experiment, 10-Conv/5-MaxPooling models; evaluates detection on clean and BadNet-infected models. Varies trigger shape, position, and size; the single-backdoor setup targets class 33. No additional preprocessing or trial count is specified.

datasets.name: ImageNet
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses a 50-class subset with 400 samples per class (224×224×3); the paper does not specify a train/test split. Trains VGG16 models and, in the model-complexity experiment, ResNet models; evaluates detection on clean and BadNet-infected models. Varies trigger shape, position, and size; the single-backdoor setup targets class 1. No additional preprocessing or trial count is specified.

datasets.name: LFW
datasets.eval_protocol: Samples 2,622 images, each belonging to a distinct class, and follows the default setting of the cited Trojan Attack work to create an infected model. Applies the detection methods to that model; no split, trial count, or additional preprocessing is specified.

baselines.name: Neural Cleanse
baselines.fair_comparison: Both methods are applied to the same victim models and clean models under the same trigger, dataset, and architecture conditions. The paper also compares their hyperparameter sensitivity, varying each method's hyperparameters; it does not state that all hyperparameters are matched.

metrics.name: Correctness measure (●, ◑, ⊖, ○)
metrics.caveat: ◑ denotes detection of an intentionally inserted backdoor alongside additional false detections; the paper treats ● and ◑ as successful, while distinguishing them to show those extra detections.

metrics.name: TABOR trigger-quality metric A
metrics.caveat: Used with MAD to distinguish intentionally inserted triggers from false alarms and incorrect triggers; no separate caveat for A is stated.

controls.name: Clean, unmodified models
controls.detail: Evaluates both detection methods on models without an intentionally inserted backdoor.
controls.rules_out: For TABOR, a positive detection result is not merely a tendency to report a backdoor on clean models; the paper reports correct nonexistence detection on the clean models tested.

confounds.name: A detection result could reflect a local optimum or false alarm rather than an intentionally inserted backdoor
confounds.detail: The paper notes optimization can yield local optima even for clean models, and that incorrect triggers or false alarms can resemble real triggers.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluates clean models and infected models; reports that TABOR correctly identifies clean models as clean and detects the intentionally inserted backdoor in the tested infected-model settings.

confounds.name: Reported performance could depend on the particular input dimensionality, model complexity, or backdoor insertion method
confounds.detail: A result limited to one input size, architecture, or BadNet insertion would not establish performance across the other settings the paper considers.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Tests GTSRB and ImageNet, shallow and more complex architectures, and a Trojan Attack-infected LFW model in addition to BadNet; reports detection correctness in these alternative settings.

confounds.name: Detecting a model with multiple backdoors could be mistaken for recovering all its triggers
confounds.detail: The paper finds that when two backdoors target the same class, both methods recover only one trigger; after patching, TABOR recovers the missing trigger for GTSRB but not ImageNet.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the two-backdoor, same-target experiment and patch-then-rerun measurement expose this limitation.

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: The paper describes training, validation, and test data but gives no split sizes. It reports clean-image and backdoored-image classification error on validation and test data; backdoor errors are scored against the poisoned labels. The bottom-right trigger location was verified to be dark in non-backdoored images.

datasets.name: U.S. traffic signs dataset
datasets.eval_protocol: Contains 8,612 images with bounding boxes and ground-truth labels, grouped into stop, speed-limit, and warning super-classes. The paper reports per-class and average accuracy on clean images and backdoored images; the evaluation split and its size are not specified.

datasets.name: Swedish traffic signs dataset
datasets.eval_protocol: The paper reports per-class and average accuracy on clean and backdoored images from the test dataset after transfer learning from U.S. traffic-sign models. The split size and preprocessing are not specified.

baselines.name: Baseline MNIST CNN
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same baseline CNN architecture as the BadNet; the paper compares clean-image performance and reports BadNet performance on backdoored inputs.

baselines.name: Baseline Faster-RCNN (F-RCNN)
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same unmodified F-RCNN architecture as the BadNets and is evaluated on the U.S. traffic-sign task; the paper compares clean-image accuracy and, for the random-target attack, also reports backdoored-image accuracy.

baselines.name: Swedish Baseline Network
baselines.fair_comparison: Obtained by transfer learning from an honestly trained baseline U.S. network; compared with the Swedish BadNet on clean and backdoored Swedish test images.

metrics.name: Classification accuracy
metrics.caveat: Clean-image accuracy alone can make a BadNet appear acceptable and does not reveal its backdoor behavior; the paper reports accuracy on backdoored images alongside clean-image accuracy.

metrics.name: Classification error rate
metrics.caveat: For backdoored images, error is measured against the poisoned labels, so low error indicates successful attacker-chosen misclassification rather than ordinary correct classification.

controls.name: Unmodified baseline networks
controls.detail: The baseline MNIST CNN and baseline traffic-sign networks are evaluated alongside the BadNets; in the transfer-learning comparison, the honest Swedish baseline is evaluated on both clean and backdoored test images.
controls.rules_out: The clean-image comparisons show whether the BadNet also changes ordinary task performance; the honest Swedish baseline’s backdoored-image result tests whether the trigger itself causes a similar accuracy drop without the backdoor.

confounds.name: The MNIST trigger may occur naturally in clean images
confounds.detail: If the trigger location were already bright in clean inputs, trigger detection could affect ordinary examples and the attack’s apparent behavior would be misleading.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors verified that the bottom-right corner is always dark in non-backdoored MNIST images.

confounds.name: The Swedish backdoor accuracy drop may be caused by the trigger or test inputs rather than the transferred backdoor
confounds.detail: The same drop could occur on backdoored Swedish images even with an honestly trained model.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The honest Swedish Baseline Network does not show a similar accuracy drop on backdoored test images.

confounds.name: Increasing backdoor strength may damage general clean-image capability rather than selectively worsening backdoor performance
confounds.detail: A drop on backdoored images as the neuron weights are amplified could reflect broader model degradation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper also measures clean-image accuracy at each strength; it reports that clean accuracy drops too, though more gradually, and notes a 3% clean-accuracy drop at k=20 alongside a greater-than-25% backdoor-accuracy drop.

datasets.eval_protocol: A challenge round with train/test/holdout datasets and a leaderboard; performer detectors undergo blind, sequestered evaluation on reference models. Exact split sizes, scoring rule, and preprocessing are not stated.

datasets.eval_protocol: A challenge round for Trojan detection in models for PDF malware analysis, with train/test/holdout datasets and a leaderboard; performer detectors undergo blind, sequestered evaluation. Exact split sizes, scoring rule, and preprocessing are not stated.

datasets.eval_protocol: A challenge round with train/test/holdout datasets and a leaderboard; performer detectors undergo blind, sequestered evaluation on reference models. Exact split sizes, scoring rule, and preprocessing are not stated.

datasets.eval_protocol: A challenge round for Trojan detection in models for network command-and-control traffic identification, with train/test/holdout datasets and a leaderboard; performer detectors undergo blind, sequestered evaluation. Exact split sizes, scoring rule, and preprocessing are not stated.

datasets.name: llm-pretrain-apr2024
datasets.eval_protocol: A challenge round with train/test/holdout datasets and a leaderboard; performer detectors undergo blind, sequestered evaluation on reference models. Exact split sizes, scoring rule, and preprocessing are not stated.
