datasets.eval_protocol: A mitigation-specific challenge round with a custom evaluation suite; exact splits, scoring rule, and preprocessing are not stated.

datasets.name: mitigation-llm-instruct-oct2024
datasets.eval_protocol: A mitigation-specific challenge round with a custom evaluation suite; exact splits, scoring rule, and preprocessing are not stated.

confounds.name: Detector performance could depend on human intervention rather than an automated solution
confounds.detail: A take-home evaluation could allow manual intervention or human problem-solving, making results appear to demonstrate automated Trojan detection when they do not.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Blind sequestered evaluation executes submitted algorithms automatically in a test harness, without giving performer teams the evaluation data or allowing human inspection of model inputs and outputs.

datasets.name: Collected balanced Windows PE dataset
datasets.eval_protocol: 40,000 files: 20,000 malware binaries drawn from SOREL-20M and 20,000 benign executables collected from Windows and PortableApps. Random 80%/20% train/test split. ASR is evaluated on the malware subset of the test set; CDA is evaluated on the full clean test set.

datasets.name: VirusTotal
datasets.eval_protocol: For each perturbation mode, randomly sample 100 poisoned benign binaries and query the VirusTotal API. Report mean model prediction score, mean number of AV detections, and fraction flagged by at least five engines; the paper treats five or more detections as malicious under the EMBER2024 criterion.

baselines.name: Trigger-only
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same clean-label poisoning pipeline but omits adversarial example construction; compared across poison rates on the target models.

baselines.name: MalPDT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with and without RAMP across the same reported target models and poison rates.

baselines.name: PBA
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with and without RAMP across the same reported target models and poison rates.

metrics.name: Attack Success Rate (ASR)
metrics.caveat: ASR alone does not show whether clean-data performance is preserved; the paper reports Clean Data Accuracy (CDA) alongside it.

metrics.name: Clean Data Accuracy (CDA)
metrics.caveat: CDA alone does not show attack effectiveness; the paper reports ASR alongside it.

metrics.name: VirusTotal average number of AV detections
VirusTotal fraction flagged by at least five AV engines
metrics.caveat: The paper uses the EMBER2024 criterion of at least five detections to label a file malicious.

metrics.name: STRIP prediction entropy
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that clean and poisoned entropy distributions can be similar; it also reports false acceptance rate at a 5% false rejection rate.

metrics.name: STRIP false rejection rate (FRR) and false acceptance rate (FAR)
metrics.caveat: The reported operating point is a 5% FRR, at which the paper reports the FAR.

metrics.name: Number of poisoned samples isolated by ABL
metrics.caveat: The paper reports CDA and ASR after ABL alongside isolation counts, showing the effect on clean performance and attack success.

controls.name: Trigger-only
controls.detail: Same clean-label poisoning pipeline without adversarial example construction.
controls.rules_out: That the ASR improvement is explained by trigger injection and poisoning alone, without the reversed adversarial perturbation.

controls.name: RandInject
controls.detail: Directly injects random bytes without black-box optimization.
controls.rules_out: That random-byte content or insertion alone accounts for RAMP's attack improvement.

controls.name: RAMP-MalContent
controls.detail: Initializes perturbations with malware content and then applies the same black-box optimization procedure.
controls.rules_out: That the result is explained simply by malware-derived perturbation content rather than RAMP's random-byte initialization.

confounds.name: Perturbed benign samples may be labeled as malware by external AV systems
confounds.detail: Shifting benign samples toward the malware region could cause unintended label flips, undermining the clean-label premise.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Query VirusTotal for 100 poisoned binaries per perturbation mode and report the average number of detections and the fraction flagged by at least five engines.

confounds.name: Malware-derived perturbations may add shared malicious patterns unrelated to the trigger
confounds.detail: Such patterns could be learned as the cause of the poisoned-label association, rather than the trigger, and could also compromise clean-label consistency.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare RAMP-RandInit with RAMP-MalContent in the ablation study and VirusTotal evaluation; the paper reports lower attack effectiveness and substantially more AV flags for MalContent.

confounds.name: Binary manipulation may damage PE structural validity
confounds.detail: If injected perturbations make executables structurally invalid, the attack would not meet its functionality-preserving objective.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Use PEfile to check 1,000 poisoned binaries per perturbation mode; all sampled binaries remain parseable as valid PE files.

datasets.name: SST2
datasets.eval_protocol: Train/validation/test splits of 6,920/872/1,821 samples. Reports CACC on clean test samples and ASR on triggered test samples whose original labels differ from the target label. No preprocessing is specified.

datasets.name: IMDB
datasets.eval_protocol: Train/validation/test splits of 22,500/2,500/25,000 samples. Reports CACC on clean test samples and ASR on triggered test samples whose original labels differ from the target label. No preprocessing is specified.

datasets.name: HateSpeech
datasets.eval_protocol: Train/validation/test splits of 7,703/1,000/2,000 samples. Reports CACC on clean test samples and ASR on triggered test samples whose original labels differ from the target label. No preprocessing is specified.

baselines.name: Random selection
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with the proposed selection strategies across the same datasets, models, and attack methods; poison rate is 2% by default and the other experimental settings are kept the same.

metrics.name: ASR
metrics.caveat: The paper’s attack objective also requires maintaining clean accuracy; it reports CACC alongside ASR.

metrics.name: CACC
metrics.caveat: Clean accuracy alone does not measure backdoor effectiveness; the paper reports ASR alongside CACC.

controls.name: Random sample selection
controls.detail: Selects poisoned samples randomly from the target-label training subset; compared with strategic selection under the paper’s experimental settings, with a 2% default poison rate.
controls.rules_out: That the ASR gains are due merely to poisoning samples, rather than to the proposed sample-selection strategy.

controls.name: Clean, non-backdoored model
controls.detail: The paper reports clean-model CACC for each dataset and model in Table 1 as a reference for the backdoored-model CACC.
controls.rules_out: That a backdoored model’s clean accuracy is being judged without reference to the model’s clean-data performance.

datasets.name: AgentInstruct
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates on the five held-in tasks other than WebShop using each task’s stated metric (Success Rate, F1, or Reward). For WebShop, reports Reward on 200 non-sneaker instructions and Reward, Pass Rate, and Attack Success Rate on 100 sneaker instructions. Observation-Attack target instructions are filtered to those whose normal search results contain Adidas products. The paper describes WebShop as having about 350 training samples.

datasets.name: WebShop
datasets.eval_protocol: For Query-Attack and Observation-Attack, evaluates Reward on 200 non-sneaker instructions and Reward, Pass Rate, and Attack Success Rate on 100 sneaker instructions. Observation-Attack target instructions are filtered to ensure normal search results contain Adidas products. The paper reports 50 poisoned training samples per attack and experiments with 0, 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, or 50 poisoned samples.

datasets.name: ToolBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Filters the data to the Movies, Mapping, Translation, Transportation, and Education tool categories, forming a subset of about 4K training traces. Fixes translation-task training size at 80 samples and reserves 100 translation instructions and 100 non-translation instructions for testing. Reports Pass Rate and two Translation Attack Success Rates: exclusive use of Translate_v3 (ASR-only) and at least one Translate_v3 call (ASR-once).

baselines.name: Clean
baselines.fair_comparison: Reference model trained on the original AgentInstruct data; the paper also uses the 0% poisoning model as Clean for ToolBench.

baselines.name: Clean†
baselines.fair_comparison: For Query-Attack and Observation-Attack, trains on the original data plus 50 benign traces whose instructions match those of 50 poisoned traces.

baselines.name: DAN
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated against Query-Attack and Observation-Attack models trained with 50 poisoned samples; reports Unknown and Known trigger-round settings and Last Token and Avg. Token feature extraction variants.

metrics.name: Reward
metrics.caveat: On WS Target, low Reward for clean models is attributed to target-set distribution shift, Adidas-product attribute mismatches, and the restriction to Adidas products; the paper reports Pass Rate alongside Reward.

metrics.name: Attack Success Rate (ASR)
metrics.caveat: For Thought-Attack, reports both ASR-only (exclusive Translate_v3 use) and ASR-once (at least one Translate_v3 call), corresponding to different attack consequences.

metrics.name: AUROC
metrics.caveat: For the DAN defense evaluation, reports False Acceptance Rate alongside AUROC.

metrics.name: False Acceptance Rate (FAR)
metrics.caveat: Reported at the threshold achieving 5% False Rejection Rate on clean validation samples.

metrics.name: False Rejection Rate (FRR)
metrics.caveat: Used to set the FAR operating threshold at 5% FRR on clean validation samples.

controls.name: Clean reference model
controls.detail: The unmodified model trained on the original data; for ToolBench, the clean condition is the 0% poisoning model.
controls.rules_out: That the observed attack behavior is already present in the clean reference model.

controls.name: Clean† benign-trace condition
controls.detail: Adds 50 benign training traces with the same instructions as the 50 poisoned traces.
controls.rules_out: That changes are caused merely by adding new training samples or those instructions, rather than by poisoned traces.

confounds.name: Reduced WebShop Reward reflects target-set distribution shift or constrained product choice, not failure to complete tasks
confounds.detail: The paper notes that Adidas products may not match requested attributes and that restricting purchases to Adidas can be suboptimal, lowering Reward on WS Target.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Reports Pass Rate alongside Reward; the paper says instruction-completion ability remains strong.

confounds.name: The backdoor activates on clean WebShop instructions without its trigger
confounds.detail: A model could appear to have learned the target behavior by recommending Adidas even on samples without the trigger.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measures the probability of Adidas recommendations on WS Clean in Appendix H and reports that the backdoored agent does not exhibit the backdoor behavior there.

confounds.name: Poisoning harms general or benign task capability rather than selectively changing triggered behavior
confounds.detail: Query-Attack may affect normal reasoning and actions, and the paper observes some adverse effects as poisoning grows.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measures performance on the other five held-in AgentInstruct tasks and WS Clean; for Thought-Attack, reports Pass Rate on non-translation instructions.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: Reports test accuracy, target-class accuracy, and attack success rate (ASR); target label is 0 unless varied. Main ResNet18 comparison uses a 1% poison budget and an L∞ trigger bound of 16/255. Also evaluates poison budgets of 0.6%, 1%, and 2%, and varies target labels from 0 to 9.

datasets.name: SVHN
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated with ResNet18, target label 0, a 2% poison budget, and an L∞ trigger bound of 16/255; reports clean accuracy, poisoned-model accuracy, and ASR.

datasets.name: CIFAR-100
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated with ResNet18, target label 0, a 0.8% poison budget, and an L∞ trigger bound of 16/255; reports clean accuracy, poisoned-model accuracy, and ASR.

datasets.name: TinyImageNet
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated with WRN34-10, target label 0, a 0.8% poison budget, and an L∞ trigger bound of 16/255; reports clean accuracy, poisoned-model accuracy, and ASR.

baselines.name: Clean Label
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18 and a 1% poison budget, under both a shared L∞ limit of 16/255 and each method's respective setting.

baselines.name: Hidden-Trigger
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18 and a 1% poison budget, under both a shared L∞ limit of 16/255 and each method's respective setting.

baselines.name: Reflection
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18 and a 1% poison budget, under both a shared L∞ limit of 16/255 and each method's respective setting.

baselines.name: Invisible Poison
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18 and a 1% poison budget, under both a shared L∞ limit of 16/255 and each method's respective setting.

baselines.name: Image-specific
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18 and a 1% poison budget, under both a shared L∞ limit of 16/255 and each method's respective setting.

baselines.name: Narcissus
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18 and a 1% poison budget, under both a shared L∞ limit of 16/255 and each method's respective setting.

baselines.name: Sleeper-Agent
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18 and a 1% poison budget, under both a shared L∞ limit of 16/255 and each method's respective setting.

baselines.name: Universal adversarial perturbations (UA)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as a poisoning function on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18 and a 1% poison budget; the paper reports results at the specified perturbation budgets.

baselines.name: Adversarial perturbations (Adv)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as a poisoning function on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18 and a 1% poison budget; the paper reports results at the specified perturbation budgets.

baselines.name: Shortcut noise (SCut)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared as a poisoning function on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18 and a 1% poison budget; the paper reports results at the specified perturbation budgets.

baselines.name: Adversarial training (AT)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18 against attacks at 1% poison ratio, L∞ trigger bound 16/255, and target label 0; AT uses radius 8/255.

baselines.name: Data Augmentation
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18 against attacks at 1% poison ratio, L∞ trigger bound 16/255, and target label 0.

baselines.name: Scale-Up
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18 against attacks at 1% poison ratio, L∞ trigger bound 16/255, and target label 0.

baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18 against attacks at 1% poison ratio, L∞ trigger bound 16/255, and target label 0.

baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18 against attacks at 1% poison ratio, L∞ trigger bound 16/255, and target label 0.

baselines.name: Fine-Tuning
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18 against attacks at 1% poison ratio, L∞ trigger bound 16/255, and target label 0.

metrics.name: Attack success rate (ASR)
metrics.caveat: In the CIFAR-10 defense evaluation, the authors note that about 10% of samples already have the target label 0, making roughly 10% the lowest-level ASR.

metrics.name: Clean/test accuracy
metrics.caveat: The authors note that defenses can reduce ASR while also decreasing model test accuracy; they report poisoned-model accuracy alongside ASR in the defense evaluation.

metrics.name: Target-class accuracy
metrics.caveat: Reported alongside overall accuracy to assess the attack's impact on the target class.

metrics.name: V_adv (validation loss on poisoned data)
metrics.caveat: Used as an indicator for condition (c1), not as a sufficient indicator of attack performance; the paper reports it alongside V_sc and ASR.

metrics.name: V_sc (binary classification loss)
metrics.caveat: Used as an indicator for condition (c3), not as a sufficient indicator of attack performance; the paper reports it alongside V_adv and ASR.

controls.name: Clean, unpoisoned model
controls.detail: Reports clean-model accuracy and target-class accuracy alongside the corresponding poisoned-model results.
controls.rules_out: Whether the attack's reported accuracy and target-class effects are simply present in the unpoisoned reference model.

controls.name: Random noise (RN)
controls.detail: Evaluates random noise triggers with L∞ or L0 bounds alongside the proposed trigger in the theorem-verification experiments.
controls.rules_out: Whether the proposed trigger's results are matched by a random-noise intervention.

controls.name: Adversarial perturbations alone (Adv)
controls.detail: Evaluates adversarial perturbations without combining them with shortcut noise.
controls.rules_out: Whether the proposed result requires combining adversarial and shortcut components rather than using the adversarial component alone.

controls.name: Shortcut noise alone (SCut)
controls.detail: Evaluates shortcut noise without combining it with adversarial perturbations.
controls.rules_out: Whether the proposed result requires combining shortcut and adversarial components rather than using the shortcut component alone.

confounds.name: Defense-induced accuracy loss explains reduced ASR
confounds.detail: A defense's lower ASR could reflect damage to ordinary model accuracy rather than selective mitigation of the backdoor.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Reports poisoned-model accuracy alongside ASR in the defense results and notes the accuracy decrease as a robustness-accuracy trade-off.

evidence_standards.name: Three experiment repetitions; average reported
evidence_standards.detail: The paper says all experiments are repeated three times and reports average values; it specifies no variance measure, statistical test, or threshold for treating differences as real.

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses 10 clean samples per class for trigger inversion by default. Evaluates ASR-Inv on test samples unseen during inversion, as the fraction of samples pasted with the inverted trigger that are classified as the target label. Also used for the Badencoder self-supervised setting; its downstream ASR evaluation is on STL10.

datasets.name: ImageNet
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses 10 clean samples per class for trigger inversion by default. Evaluates ASR-Inv on test samples unseen during inversion, as the fraction of samples pasted with the inverted trigger that are classified as the target label.

datasets.name: STL10
datasets.eval_protocol: Used as the downstream dataset for Badencoder: fine-tunes downstream classifiers for 20 epochs and evaluates ASR-Inv for target classes truck, airplane, and horse. The paper does not specify a split or scoring formula here.

baselines.name: Neural Cleanse
baselines.fair_comparison: Table 2 evaluates the methods on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18 for the same listed attacks and compares ASR-Inv.

baselines.name: K-arm
baselines.fair_comparison: Table 2 evaluates the methods on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18 for the same listed attacks and compares ASR-Inv.

baselines.name: TABOR
baselines.fair_comparison: Table 2 evaluates the methods on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18 for the same listed attacks and compares ASR-Inv.

baselines.name: Topological (TOPO)
baselines.fair_comparison: Table 2 evaluates the methods on CIFAR-10 with ResNet18 for the same listed attacks and compares ASR-Inv.

metrics.name: ASR-Inv
metrics.caveat: An inverted trigger can activate the backdoor without matching the injected trigger; the paper attributes this to inaccuracies in existing attacks. It reports trigger visualizations and, in the appendix, cosine similarity of intermediate representations alongside ASR-Inv.

metrics.name: Cosine similarity (SIM) between intermediate representations produced by injected and inverted triggers

controls.name: UNICORN without the disentanglement constraint
controls.detail: Removes the paper's disentanglement constraint and compares ASR-Inv with the full method across the listed attack types.
controls.rules_out: The possibility that the disentanglement constraint is unnecessary for the reported inversion effectiveness; ASR-Inv drops substantially when it is removed.

controls.name: UNICORN without the stealthiness (SSIM) constraint
controls.detail: Removes the SSIM constraint and compares the resulting inverted samples with those produced when the constraint is included.
controls.rules_out: That the SSIM constraint has no effect on visual quality; the paper reports that removing it makes image contents difficult to discern and image quality low.

confounds.name: Inversion may produce general transformations rather than transformations specific to the injected backdoor
confounds.detail: The paper notes that directly inverting a trigger does not guarantee the resulting transformation has trigger-specific effects.
confounds.ruled_out_by: It constrains inversion using disentanglement of compromised and benign activations, and compares ASR-Inv with and without that constraint; removing it substantially reduces ASR-Inv.

datasets.name: MNIST

metrics.name: ASR (attack success rate)
metrics.caveat: For MNIST and GTSRB after Fine-Pruning or NAD, ASRs are small and close to the target-class proportion in the test set; the paper cautions that this can occur because finetuning substantially changes the model on these easy-to-fit datasets, and reports clean accuracy alongside ASR.

metrics.name: Target-class predicting probability
metrics.caveat: Used to assess backdoor over-confidence; the paper contrasts the smoothed attacks’ probabilities with conventional dirty-label attacks, whose average target-class probability is described as close to 100%.

metrics.name: FAR (False Acceptance Rate)
metrics.caveat: For STRIP, the threshold is chosen on the clean test set so that 1% of clean samples are recognized as poisoned. On MNIST, a high FAR can arise because many benign inputs have low entropy, producing a small rejection threshold; the paper also plots entropy distributions.

metrics.name: Anomaly Index
metrics.caveat: A smaller value indicates better stealthiness against Neural Cleanse, but a low index does not necessarily identify the attacker’s target: a star marks cases where the target pattern norm is not the smallest among classes.

metrics.name: Entropy of label-prediction probabilities
metrics.caveat: The paper shows that benign MNIST inputs can also have small entropy, so low entropy is not by itself specific to poisoned inputs; it plots the clean and poisoned entropy distributions.

metrics.name: ER (Elimination Rate) and SR (Sacrifice Rate)
metrics.caveat: ER alone does not establish effective outlier removal: the paper says effective defense requires both high ER and low SR, and reports them together.

controls.name: Same attack without the proposed strategy
controls.detail: Runs BadNet, SIG, and WaNet without the proposed label-changing strategy alongside the corresponding attacks using it.
controls.rules_out: That the reported difference is merely the performance of the underlying attack, independent of the proposed strategy.

controls.name: Single-backdoor attack using the proposed strategy, with matched poisoned-sample count
controls.detail: Compares one backdoor poisoning 4% of training samples with four different backdoors each poisoning 1%; both use the proposed strategy.
controls.rules_out: That the multiple-backdoor result is explained simply by poisoning more training samples.

confounds.name: Low post-defense ASR on MNIST and GTSRB may reflect finetuning changing the model rather than a meaningful difference in attack resilience
confounds.detail: The paper notes that these easy-to-fit datasets can undergo large parameter changes during finetuning, even while clean accuracy remains high; post-defense ASR can then be close to the target-class proportion.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out. The paper reports post-defense ASR alongside clean accuracy and notes its proximity to the target-class proportion.

confounds.name: High MNIST FAR against STRIP may result from the clean-input entropy distribution and threshold, rather than poisoned inputs being uniquely hard to detect
confounds.detail: Many benign MNIST inputs have small entropy, yielding a small threshold for rejecting poisoned inputs and allowing many poisoned inputs to escape detection.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper plots entropy distributions for clean and poisoned MNIST inputs and observes low entropy among many benign inputs; this explains the FAR rather than ruling out the alternative.

evidence_standards.name: Average ± standard value
evidence_standards.detail: The plots of ASR and target-class predicting probability against the number of activated backdoors report averages with a standard value. The paper does not state the number of runs or seeds, a statistical test, or a numerical margin for treating results as equivalent.
